Ubi deprimenda vox, ubi tollenda, accentus eodem in verbo repetiti docent. Fere enim modulata, ac cantatrix est gentis hujus locutio. Ad condiscendam pronunciationem soli accentus vix sufficiunt. Raregrágremarachiñ Oahérkaikiñ. Nomina sunt Abiponum. Grcáuagyégarigé Miserere mei. ... En viginti literarum verba! Monosyllaba haud multa deprehendas.

new_statements.quote: Accentuum, punctulorumque religiosissime habenda est ratio. Idem enim vocabulum punctulo omisso, variatóve accentu aliud atque aliud denotat. Sic: Heét fugio. Hëet loquor. Háten despicio. Hatén collimando attingo. Vocabulis longioribus, quae ex decem, ex viginti, ex pluribus literis componuntur, haec lingua abundat. Ubi deprimenda vox, ubi tollenda, accentus eodem in verbo repetiti docent. Fere enim modulata, ac cantatrix est gentis hujus locutio. Ad condiscendam pronunciationem soli accentus vix sufficiunt.
new_statements.translation: The accents and little dots must be observed most scrupulously, for the same word with the dot omitted or the accent changed means one thing and then another. Thus: Heét 'I flee', Hëet 'I speak'; Háten 'I despise', Hatén 'I hit the mark (aiming)'. This language abounds in longer words composed of ten, twenty or more letters. Where the voice is to be lowered and where raised, accents repeated in the same word show; for the speech of this nation is almost modulated and singing. Accents alone hardly suffice for learning the pronunciation.
new_statements.citation: Dobrizhoffer, Martin. 1784. Historia de Abiponibus equestri, bellicosaque Paraquariae natione. Tomus II. Viennae: Typis Josephi Nob. de Kurzbek.
new_statements.locator: Tomus II, p. 165 (chapter on the Abipón language); English transl. 1822 vol. II p. 161
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Files checked under ( present and accurate). Ubi deprimenda vox, ubi tollenda, accentus eodem in verbo repetiti docent. Fere enim modulata, ac cantatrix est gentis hujus locutio. Ad condiscendam pronunciationem soli accentus vix sufficiunt.'), followed by the multi-accent examples Hamihégemkin, Debáyakaikin, Oahérkaikin, Grcáuag…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only first-hand observer (Dobrizhoffer, 18 years among the Abipón) states that accent placement is distinctive: words otherwise identical differ in meaning by accent alone (Háten vs Hatén), and long words carry several marked accents indicating pitch rises and falls; he gives no positional rule. The comparatist Adam (1899: 22, §49), working from Dobrizhoffer's and Brigniel's transcriptions for the whole Guaicurú family, generalises that the accent 'regularly' falls on the final vowel (most often) or on the penult (with the final vowel then weakened and apocopated). Net provisional reading: accent not fixed, predominantly final with penultimate alternatives, lexically contrastive per Dobrizhoffer's minimal pair.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Dobrizhoffer notes several accents written within one long word marking where the voice rises and falls (e.g. Hamihégemkin, Debáyakaikin, Oahérkaikin, Grcáuagyégarigé), suggesting multiple prominences/pitch movements, but no rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; Dobrizhoffer adds that interrogation may be signalled 'solo accentu, vocisque elatione' (by accent and raising of the voice alone), a phrase-level use. Adam 1899 warns that the missionaries very often omitted the accent mark.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms in missionary orthography (acute accent marks); Dobrizhoffer's description mixes word accent with an overall 'singing' intonation, so the accent may be partly pitch-based. Adam's final/penult statement (1899 §49, p. 22: 'Régulièrement l'accent porte ou sur la dernière voyelle ce qui est le plus fréquent, ou sur la voyelle pénultième, et dans ce cas la voyelle finale est atténuée, partant sujette à apocope. Très souvent, les Missionnaires ont omis l'accent.') is family-wide (Abipone, Mocoví, Toba, Mbayá), not Abipón-specific. The modern restatement (Najlis 1966 I: 13-20) was not accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: Dobrizhoffer describes the Abipón of the Jesuit reductions of the Chaco santafesino (mid-18th c; he names the Riikahé, Nakaigetergehé and Yaaukanigá divisions) = Glottolog abip1241, no sub-dialect distinguished. Adam 1899's accent statement is a family-level generalisation over Abipón, Mocoví (moco1246), Toba (toba1269) and Mbayá (mbay1241 / Kadiwéu) missionary materials, not Abipón-specific.

sources.note: Accents (and diacritic dots) must be observed most scrupulously because the same word with the accent varied means something else: Heét 'I flee' vs Hëet 'I speak', Háten 'I despise' vs Hatén 'I hit the mark'; accents repeated within long words show where the voice is raised and lowered; speech is 'modulated and singing'. Also (p. ~186) interrogation can be marked by accent/raising of the voice alone. No positional rule given.
